parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use the definitions of speed $v$, frequency $f$ and wavelength $\lambda$ to derive the wave equation $$v = f\lambda.$$

markscheme_points.text: wavelength: • wavelength = distance between successive / adjacent in phase points / wavefronts / crests / troughs • λ = d / (number of) oscillations frequency: • frequency = (number of) oscillations / cycles crests / troughs / wavefronts (passing a point) per unit time • f = (number of) oscillations / t One correct point from either list

One correct point from both lists and speed = distance / time and one of: • wavelength × frequency (= distance per unit time) = speed • [(number of) oscillations / t] × [d / (number of) oscillations] = fλ • v (= d / t) = λ / (1/f) = fλ or v (= d / t) = λ / T = fλ

hints: Hint 1: Start by reminding yourself what each word means in plain language - what distance does speed involve, what distance does one wavelength represent, and what time does one frequency count?
Hint 2: Think about the time for just one complete oscillation and the distance the wave has travelled in that time, then combine them using speed = distance / time.
parts.proper_answer: Speed $v = d/t$, wavelength $\lambda$ = distance for one oscillation, frequency $f$ = oscillations per unit time $= 1/T$. In time $T = 1/f$ wave travels distance $\lambda$, so $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what speed, wavelength and frequency really mean**
You can think of a wave as a moving pattern. Speed is always distance travelled divided by time taken, so $$v = \frac{d}{t}$$. Wavelength $\lambda$ is the length of one complete pattern - the distance between two neighbouring crests, or the distance the wave moves during one oscillation. Frequency $f$ is how many oscillations happen each second.

Step 2: **Link frequency to the time for one wave**
If $f$ oscillations happen in 1 s, then the time for one oscillation, the period $T$, is $$T = \frac{1}{f}$$. In that time $T$ the wave must have moved forward by exactly one wavelength $\lambda$.

Step 3: **Put distance and time into speed**
Now use speed = distance / time for this special distance and time: $$v = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$. Since $1/T = f$, this becomes $$v = f\lambda$$. That is the wave equation - distance per wave times waves per second gives distance per second.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A source of sound waves of frequency $236\text{ Hz}$ is travelling at a constant velocity of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

A stationary observer has a microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO). The microphone detects the sound waves as the source moves directly towards the observer.

The resulting trace on the CRO is shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The time-base on the CRO is set to $1.0\text{ ms div}^{-1}$.
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound waves detected by the microphone.
hints: Hint 1: On a CRO the horizontal axis is time. Count how many horizontal divisions make up one complete sine wave from peak to next peak.
Hint 2: Convert that number of divisions into seconds using the 1.0 ms per division setting, then remember how period and frequency are linked.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from the trace**
Pick two matching points, for example one peak to the next peak. On Fig. 5.1 one full cycle spans 4 large divisions. Each division is $1.0\text{ ms}$, so $$T = 4.0 \times 1.0\text{ ms} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$. It helps to measure over more than one cycle if you can to reduce reading error, but here one cycle is clear.

Step 2: **Convert period to observed frequency**
Frequency is oscillations per second: $$f_o = \frac{1}{T}$$. So $$f_o = \frac{1}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}} = 250\text{ Hz}$$. Notice this is higher than the source $236\text{ Hz}$ because the source is moving towards you - a classic Doppler shift.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the speed of the sound in air.
hints: Hint 1: You now know the source frequency and the higher frequency heard by the stationary observer when the source approaches. Which Doppler formula connects these two frequencies to the source speed and wave speed?
Hint 2: Substitute $f_s = 236\text{ Hz}$, $f_o = 250\text{ Hz}$ and $v_s = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ into that relation and rearrange algebraically to isolate the wave speed $v$ before calculating.
parts.proper_answer: For source approaching: $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$. $250 = 236v/(v-20)$ giving $v = 360\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (2 s.f.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture why the frequency is raised**
The source chases its own waves, so the waves ahead of it are squashed together. Wavelength in front is shortened, so a stationary observer meets more waves per second. For a source speed $v_s$ moving towards the observer: $$f_o = f_s \frac{v}{v - v_s}$$ where $v$ is the speed of sound.

Step 2: **Solve for the speed of sound**
Insert the numbers you know: $f_s = 236\text{ Hz}$, $f_o = 250\text{ Hz}$, $v_s = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$250 = 236 \times \frac{v}{v - 20}$$. Rearrange: $$250(v-20) = 236v$$ $$250v - 5000 = 236v$$ $$14v = 5000$$. So $$v = \frac{5000}{14} \approx 360\text{ m s}^{-1}$$. This is a sensible order of magnitude for sound in air.
